entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jordanes, also known as Jordanis or Jornandes, was a pivotal 6th-century Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent whose historical writings became indispensable for understanding the Goths and the broader Late Antique world. Active around 551 CE, his two surviving works, the *Romana* (a summary of world history) and the far more significant *Getica* (*De origine actibusque Getarum* or 'On the Origin and Deeds of the Getae/Goths'), provided a unique, if often biased, account of Gothic origins, migrations, and interactions with the Roman Empire. He is critical not only for preserving fragments of lost historical works but also for shaping the medieval and modern perception of the 'barbarian' peoples who reshaped Europe.

The *Getica* is primarily an abridgement of the much larger, now lost, twelve-volume *Historia Gothorum* by the Roman statesman Cassiodorus, commissioned by Theodoric the Great. Jordanes completed his summary in Constantinople, likely in 551 CE, in just three days, according to his own account, using Cassiodorus' work and other sources. His narrative traces the Goths from their mythical Scandinavian origins, through their migrations across Scythia, their encounters with the Huns under Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451 CE, and their establishment of kingdoms in Italy and Gaul. Despite its brevity and potential for misinterpretation due to its condensed nature and Romanizing perspective, the *Getica* offers invaluable details on Gothic kings, customs, and military campaigns that would otherwise be entirely lost.
